design_detail: Commentary (Drug and Alcohol Review 2022;41(7):1493–1498; received 12 May 2022, revised 19 June 2022, accepted 25 June 2022), four authors. About two and a half printed pages of text in six numbered sections (introduction; vaping and smoking cessation; vaping as a gateway to smoking; comparative harms of vaping and smoking; net public health effects of vaping; conclusion), one figure (US high-school smoking and vaping trends, drawn from CDC youth survey data), 54 references and a conflict-of-interest statement; no funding statement. No data, methods or search. Its target is the 2022 report to the Australian Department of Health by Banks and colleagues, 'Electronic cigarettes and health outcomes: systematic review of global evidence' (its reference 1, not read), the report on which the 2023 journal article in this library is based (card sc_banks_2023); the 2023 article appeared later and is not discussed. Every study cited is known here only as this commentary describes it. Commentary appraised with the editors' checklist.
can_establish: What four Australian authors argued in 2022 against the Australian report's conclusions and methods: that it did not compare the harms of vaping with those of continuing to smoke, did not weigh net population effects, underrated the trial evidence on stopping smoking, read the link between youth vaping and later smoking as causal while setting aside observational evidence on quitting, and gave weight to self-reported nicotine-only cases in the 2019 lung-injury outbreak; and which evidence they cite for each point.
cannot_establish: Whether the report's conclusions are wrong (the commentary appraises none of the evidence it cites and describes no search); how much less harmful vaping is than smoking, or what vaping does to rates of heart disease, lung disease or cancer (it cites no study of disease incidence, and its cancer figure is a modelled estimate as cited); and whether the 2023 journal article answered or changed any of the points (not discussed).

sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; the authors say they summarise evidence inconsistent with the review's main findings (Introduction, 4th paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: The 54 references are chosen to set out evidence against the report. For the health effects of switching from smoking, seven of the nine human studies or reviews cited for cardiovascular and respiratory benefit (references 35, 36 and 38 to 42) and one of the two cell studies (reference 44) share authors: at least one of Polosa, Caponnetto, Cibella, Campagna, Morjaria and Caruso appears in each author list as printed; the two others are a four-week switching study (reference 37) and an online survey of airway infections (reference 43). Cancer risk is cited to two studies that, by their titles, estimate risk from emissions (references 49 and 50); youth trends to US survey data and simulation models; quitting to trials, a network meta-analysis, reviews of cohort studies and population surveys. No study of the incidence of heart attack, stroke, chronic lung disease or cancer in people who vape is cited.

exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, except that the lung-injury paragraph turns on whether people who reported using only nicotine products had also used THC products (Comparative harms, 10th paragraph).

comparison.controls: No comparison of its own. The commentary argues that a meaningful assessment of the risk of vaping nicotine compares it with the much greater risk of continuing to smoke, because most people who vape frequently are current or former smokers who could not stop by other methods (Comparative harms, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). The journal version of the review it critiques takes people who neither smoke nor vape as the main comparison and gives its reasons (card sc_banks_2023).

outcomes.operationalization: Harm is argued from the toxicant content of aerosol against smoke, exposure biomarkers, short-term cardiovascular and respiratory measures after switching, cell studies and modelled cancer potency; the net public health effect from simulation models; effectiveness for quitting from trials, meta-analyses and surveys.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. Figures as cited: the 2021 Cochrane review, moderate-certainty evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes increase quit rates compared with nicotine replacement therapy (RR 1.53); one trial in people unable to stop smoking by conventional methods, relative risk 6.4 (95% CI 1.5 to 27.3, p = 0.01) at 6 months against nicotine replacement; a network meta-analysis of 171 trials ranking vaping the most effective single treatment, with a wide interval; people who vape daily two to eight times more likely to stop smoking than people who smoke and do not vape; fewer than 1 in 100 adults in Australia who had never smoked vaped in the previous 12 months (2019); smoke contains over 7,000 toxic chemicals against fewer than 100 detectable chemicals in aerosols; 14% of EVALI patients denied using THC; lifetime cancer risk from vaping estimated at less than 0.5% of that from smoking; no evidence of harm in studies up to 2 years in the Cochrane review (few studies); in one US model 1.8 million premature deaths avoided and 38.9 million life-years gained from 2013 to 2060; in one UK estimate 50,000 additional people stopped smoking with a vaping product in 2017. Figure 1 labels, read from the image: past-30-day smoking among US high-school students 22.3% in 2004 and 1.9% in 2021, a decline of '1% per year' from 2004 to 2013 and '1.4% per year' from 2013 to 2021; past-30-day vaping 27.5% at its 2019 peak and 11.3% in 2021.
analysis.selective_reporting: By its own statement the commentary sets out only evidence inconsistent with the review. Harms rated in the review's 2023 journal version (card sc_banks_2023), such as dependence, poisoning, burns and acute rises in heart rate and blood pressure in people who smoke, are not discussed, and no cited study is appraised.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No data. The commentary argues, from 54 references, that the report did not compare vaping with continuing to smoke; did not consider net public health effects (all but one of the simulation models cited find benefits exceed harms); rated the trial evidence on quitting as limited where the 2021 Cochrane review rated it moderate certainty; used 'evidential double standards', reading observational associations between youth vaping and later smoking as causal while setting aside observational and population evidence on quitting, although in the authors' reading adjusted studies and population trends point to a common liability or to diversion from smoking; and gave weight to the 14% of lung-injury patients who reported only nicotine products, a self-report the authors consider unreliable. On harm it cites lower toxicant content and exposure, short-term cardiovascular and respiratory improvements after switching (mostly from studies sharing authors), cell studies and a modelled cancer risk, and it says that human studies on cardiovascular outcomes are limited and that the effect of inhaled flavourings is largely unknown.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion (p. 1495) states that, contrary to the review, the evidence suggests vaping nicotine is an effective aid to stopping smoking, substantially less harmful than smoking tobacco, diverting young people away from smoking, and likely to bring a major net public health benefit if widely available to adults in Australia who smoke. Gaps: (1) 'substantially less harmful' rests on exposure, short-term and modelled evidence, the kinds the review set aside for clinical outcomes, and no study of disease incidence is cited; (2) the diversion claim rests on population time trends and survey comparisons, associations of the kind the authors say the review over-read for the gateway; (3) the statement that lower biomarkers in people who switch confirm harm reduction is cited to two studies that, by their titles, compare exposure between groups, one of them cross-sectional (references 30 and 31); (4) the sentence on in vitro and animal studies cites two human studies (references 39 and 40, by their titles) and no animal study; (5) the overlap of authors behind most of the switching evidence is not mentioned. The 2023 journal version of the review states that the uptake findings were similar after adjusting for factors including risk-taking (Results › Smoking behaviour, 1st paragraph, in the saved PMC text read for card sc_banks_2023), which the commentary, written about the 2022 report, does not address. In the authors' favour, they acknowledge the wide interval of the network meta-analysis, the mixed results of observational cohorts, limited human evidence on cardiovascular outcomes, possible risk from nicotine in people with heart disease, the unknown effects of flavourings and the small number of trials followed to 2 years.

timeline.event: BMJ analysis questioning the evidence behind the 2015 English report and the origin of its 95% figure; not cited by this commentary.
National Academies report: the starting point of the Australian review's umbrella part (card sc_banks_2023); not cited by this commentary.

Cochrane review update (Hartmann-Boyce et al., 2021): moderate-certainty evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes increase quit rates compared with nicotine replacement therapy, RR 1.53 (as cited here; no reference record; not read).

Banks et al., report to the Australian Department of Health, 'Electronic cigarettes and health outcomes: systematic review of global evidence' (dated 7 April 2022 in reference 13 of the 2023 article): the target of this commentary (reference 1 here; no reference record; not read).
UK evidence update stating that vaping carries a small fraction of the risks of smoking; published after this commentary was accepted and not cited by it.

Journal article based on the 2022 report: keeps 'limited evidence' for quitting with clinical support and 'strong evidence' for uptake of smoking by young people who vape; its text and reference list, as saved for card sc_banks_2023, do not cite this commentary.

replication.where_it_stands: A published critique of the Australian review that argues mainly about the question and the comparison (relative harm against continuing to smoke; net population effect) and about evidence standards, not with new data. On disease, it and the review do not disagree about rates of heart attack, stroke or cancer, which neither has; they disagree about which comparison and which kinds of evidence should count. No reply from the review's authors has been found: the 2023 journal article does not cite it.

funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: Dr Colin Mendelsohn was a board member of the Australian Tobacco Harm Reduction Association (ATHRA), a registered health promotion charity, from October 2017 to January 2020, and Dr Alex Wodak is a board member of ATHRA. ATHRA accepted unconditional seed funding from the vape retail industry to get established; the funding ceased in March 2019. Mendelsohn and Wodak were directors of ATHRA in March 2018 when it received a donation from Knowledge Action Change Communications, a private sector public health agency in the UK; the donation was sourced from a surplus arising from the Global Forum on Nicotine conference in May 2017. Knowledge Action Change Communications is legally separate from Knowledge Action Change (KAC). KAC has received two grants from tobacco companies: in 2012 a small development research grant from Nicoventures (then owned by British American Tobacco) to evaluate a nicotine delivery device in Scottish prisons, conducted with the Scottish Prison Service and publicly declared; and in 2018 a grant from the Foundation for a Smoke-Free World, which is funded by an annual grant from Philip Morris International, specifically for preparing The Global State of Tobacco Harm Reduction report; under the Foundation's bylaws and pledge agreement, Philip Morris International and the tobacco industry are precluded from any influence over how the Foundation spends its funds or focuses its activities. Mendelsohn is the author of the book Stop Smoking Start Vaping (Aurora Press) and has never received payments from electronic cigarette or tobacco companies; Wodak has never received payments from electronic cigarette or tobacco companies. Professors Wayne Hall and Ron Borland have no interests to declare.
funding.affiliations_note: Affiliations as printed: general practice, Sydney (Mendelsohn); St Vincent's Hospital Sydney, Alcohol and Drug Service (Wodak); University of Queensland, Centre for Youth Substance Abuse Research, Brisbane (Hall); School of Psychological Sciences, University of Melbourne (Borland). None of the four appears among the authors printed in the reference list (lists are cut after six names). Recorded as a reason to read closely, not to discount: the commentary argues for wider access to vaping for adults who smoke, and two authors held governance roles in an association that took vape-retail seed funding until March 2019; both state they have never received payments from e-cigarette or tobacco companies, and the other two authors declare no interests.

what_would_settle_it: On the comparison: long-term cohorts that report disease and death separately for people who only vape, people who smoke, people who both smoke and vape, people who stopped smoking with and without vaping, and people who never used nicotine, so that the comparison with smoking and the comparison with no nicotine can both be read from the same data. On evidence standards: a rule set in advance, applied to both quitting and starting to smoke, on which designs count as causal evidence and how residual confounding is handled. On the lung-injury outbreak: product testing linked to cases rather than self-report.

domains.note: No search or criteria; the authors set out the evidence they find inconsistent with the review.

Cited studies are described, not appraised. Some statements carry no citation (most people who vape frequently are current or former smokers; faster declines in adult smoking in the UK and US); the biomarker statement cites two group comparisons of exposure; the in vitro and animal statement cites two human studies; the overlap of authors behind most of the switching evidence is not noted.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the four authors appears among the names printed in the 54 references (author lists are cut after six names).

Firm wording ('highly implausible', 'confirmed', 'diverting young people') rests on associations, time trends and modelling; some limits are acknowledged (wide interval, mixed cohort results, limited cardiovascular evidence, unknown effects of flavourings).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how harmful vaping is compared with smoking and with using no nicotine
domains.note: Only evidence favouring vaping for adults who smoke is presented, by design; harms such as dependence, poisoning, burns and acute rises in heart rate and blood pressure are not discussed, and the comparison with people who use no nicotine is not addressed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used, as for the other critiques in this monograph (cards sc_eissenberg_2020 and sc_mckee_2015). The commentary is openly argued, says it sets out only evidence inconsistent with the review, and declares its authors' interests in detail; it is one side's case and appraises none of its sources. Cite it for what its authors argue about the review's question, comparison and evidence standards, never for the size of any harm or benefit; a claim resting only on it stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: The commentary critiques the review of vaping by Banks and colleagues funded by the Australian Department of Health, cited as the 2022 report to the Department (reference 1), whose stated aims were to examine contemporary evidence on the health outcomes of nicotine and non-nicotine e-cigarette use and to integrate it with systematic reviews on smoking uptake and cessation to guide policy and practice.

In the authors' view the review failed its aims because it did not compare the relative risk of the harms of vaping with those of cigarettes, did not consider the net public health impact of vaping, ignored evidence that vaping is effective for stopping smoking, and confused causation and correlation for youth vaping and cigarette smoking. They add that it used 'evidential double standards', accepting a causal reading of observational associations for the gateway hypothesis while rejecting similar observational evidence on cessation, and took a sceptical attitude to trials showing that vaping helps people stop smoking. They state that they summarise evidence inconsistent with the review's main findings.

Against the report's conclusion of limited evidence that, in the clinical context, freebase nicotine e-cigarettes may be more efficacious than nicotine replacement therapy, the authors cite the 2021 Cochrane review (moderate-certainty evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes increase quit rates compared with nicotine replacement, RR 1.53), other meta-analyses that agree but differ in confidence, one trial in people unable to stop by conventional methods (relative risk 6.4, 95% CI 1.5 to 27.3, at 6 months), a network meta-analysis of 171 trials ranking vaping the most effective single treatment (they note its wide interval calls for larger trials), two reviews of higher-quality cohort studies after mixed cohort results, population surveys in Australia, the US and the UK, people who vape daily being two to eight times more likely to stop, and faster declines in adult smoking where vaping is more common (no source given for the last).
key_findings.locator: 2 Vaping and smoking cessation, 1st to 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Against the report's claim of strong evidence that e-cigarettes increase uptake of smoking in people who do not smoke, particularly young people, the authors argue that the association is most likely explained by a common liability to risk-taking; that more rigorous prospective studies adjusting for shared risk factors found the association largely disappears (one paper cited, reference 18); that population studies suggest vaping diverts young people from smoking, with US youth smoking falling faster from about the time vaping became popular (Figure 1, from CDC survey data: past-30-day smoking in high-school students 22.3% in 2004 and 1.9% in 2021); that most young people who vape smoked first and most vaping by people who have never smoked is experimental and transient; and that fewer than 1 in 100 adults in Australia who had never smoked vaped in the previous 12 months in 2019.
key_findings.locator: 3 Vaping as a gateway to smoking, 1st to 5th paragraphs (the 1st begins on p. 1493); Figure 1

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the review does not address relative risk, and that a meaningful assessment of the risk of vaping nicotine should compare it with the far greater risk of continuing to smoke tobacco, because the vast majority of people who vape frequently are current or former smokers who could not stop by other methods (no source given).
key_findings.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: They write that harm reduction from vaping rests on substantially lower exposure to toxins and carcinogens in vapour than in smoke (references 28 and 29) and is confirmed by considerable reductions in biomarkers of harm in the blood, urine and saliva of people who switch (references 30 and 31); that smoke contains over 7,000 toxic chemicals and solid particulate matter while vaping aerosols generally have fewer than 100 detectable chemicals, most at far lower concentrations (reference 29); that chemicals found in vapour but not in smoke do not appear to pose a significant hazard when inhaled (a 2020 UK Committee on Toxicity statement); and that the effect of inhaled flavourings is largely unknown and could carry risk, with no harm shown so far and ongoing monitoring needed.
key_findings.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 3rd to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular: most effects of vaping are consistent with the known effects of nicotine (transiently raised pulse and blood pressure, cardiac contractility, arrhythmogenesis); nicotine may pose some risk in people with existing cardiovascular disease; cardiotoxic constituents of smoke are absent from vapour or much lower (one review, reference 34). Human studies on cardiovascular outcomes are limited; two studies showed sustained falls in blood pressure in people who switched to vaping and one showed better vascular function after 4 weeks. Respiratory: vaping is likely to be far less harmful to the lungs (a narrative review), with improved symptoms, lung function, asthma, COPD, mucociliary clearance and fewer respiratory infections reported in people who switched. In vitro and animal studies are said to find effects generally far smaller than from smoke.
key_findings.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 6th to 9th paragraphs; references 34 to 45
key_findings.note: Seven of the nine human studies or reviews cited (references 35, 36, 38 to 42) and one of the cell studies (44) share authors; the in vitro and animal sentence cites references 39 and 40, which are human studies by their titles.

key_findings.finding: The authors call it highly implausible that nicotine vaping caused the 2019 US EVALI outbreak, which they say was strongly linked to vitamin E acetate added to black-market THC vaping oils and disappeared after it was removed from the illicit supply chain (CDC, reference 46); they argue that the 14% of patients who denied using THC and had vaped nicotine do not prove a link with nicotine products, because many patients who denied vaping THC were later found to have done so and no other causal agent has been identified in nicotine e-liquids (references 47 and 48; no numbers given).
key_findings.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 10th paragraph

key_findings.finding: On the basis of the reduced number and dose of carcinogens in vapour, lifetime cancer risk from vaping has been estimated at less than 0.5% of that from smoking (references 49 and 50, which by their titles estimate cancer potency or lung cancer risk from emissions and particle measurements); the Cochrane review detected no evidence of harm in studies up to 2 years, although the studies were few and longer ones are needed.
key_findings.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 11th and 12th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that the key public health question is the net population effect, a function of the harm difference between vaping and smoking, effectiveness for stopping smoking and uptake by people who smoke and who do not; that numerous modelling studies, with one exception, conclude benefits considerably exceed harms, evaluating net effects under a wide range of assumptions about uptake, quitting and the reduction in harm compared with smoking; one US model estimated 1.8 million premature deaths avoided and 38.9 million life-years gained from 2013 to 2060, and one UK estimate put the additional people who stopped smoking with a vaping product in 2017 at 50,000.
key_findings.locator: 5 Net public health effects of vaping, 1st to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: contrary to the review's conclusions, the authors write, the evidence suggests that vaping nicotine is an effective aid to stopping smoking, that vaping is substantially less harmful than smoking tobacco, that it is diverting young people away from smoking, and that vaping by people who smoke is likely to have a major net public health benefit if widely available to adults in Australia who smoke.

The commentary does not mention the 95% figure or any other overall estimate of relative harm apart from the modelled cancer estimate, cites no study of the incidence of heart attack, stroke, chronic lung disease or cancer in people who vape, and does not engage with the reasons for the review's choice of comparison group or its exclusion of biomarker studies (both stated in the 2023 journal version, card sc_banks_2023).

Interests as printed: two authors were or are board members of the Australian Tobacco Harm Reduction Association, a registered health promotion charity that accepted unconditional seed funding from the vape retail industry until March 2019 and in March 2018 a donation from Knowledge Action Change Communications (legally separate from Knowledge Action Change, which has received a 2012 grant from Nicoventures, then owned by British American Tobacco, and a 2018 grant from the Foundation for a Smoke-Free World, funded by Philip Morris International); one author wrote the book Stop Smoking Start Vaping; both state they have never received payments from electronic cigarette or tobacco companies; the other two authors have no interests to declare. No funding statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The biomarker sentence says reduced biomarkers of harm in the blood, urine and saliva of people who switch confirm harm reduction, but the two studies cited (references 30 and 31) are, by their titles, comparisons of nicotine, carcinogen and toxicant exposure between groups, one of them cross-sectional.
reporting_issues.page: p. 1494 (4 Comparative harms, 3rd paragraph; references 30 and 31)
reporting_issues.consequence: Read as evidence of lower exposure in group comparisons, as cited, not of lower harm or of change within people who switched; the studies were not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence on in vitro and animal studies cites references 39 and 40, which by their titles are human studies (a randomised cessation trial and a follow-up of people with asthma who switched); neither of the other two (44 and 45) is, by its title, an animal study.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement about animal studies has no animal study behind it in the text.

reporting_issues.issue: 'Those who vape daily are two to eight times more likely to quit' is cited jointly to three studies (references 14 to 16), one of which is, by its title, a time-series analysis of national prevalence; which study gives which figure is not said.
reporting_issues.page: p. 1493 (2 Vaping and smoking cessation, 7th paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The range cannot be traced to a study from this text.

reporting_issues.issue: 'More rigorous prospective studies' in which the vaping-smoking association largely disappears are cited to a single paper (reference 18).
reporting_issues.page: p. 1494 (3 Vaping as a gateway, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: One re-analysis as cited, not a body of studies; not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The phrases attributed to 'the Banks review' ('limited evidence ... may be more efficacious' for quitting; 'strong evidence' for uptake of smoking) come from the 2022 report (reference 1); the 2023 journal version words these judgments differently (limited evidence that freebase nicotine e-cigarettes with clinical support are as efficacious as, or in Box 4 more efficacious than, nicotine replacement; strong evidence that young people who have never smoked or do not smoke and who use e-cigarettes are about three times as likely as those who do not to start smoking and to become regular smokers).
reporting_issues.page: p. 1493 (2 Vaping and smoking cessation, 1st paragraph; 3 Vaping as a gateway, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The critique should be described as a critique of the 2022 report; it cannot be assumed to quote the 2023 article.
